strengths: Original and thought-provoking paradigm: Reframing DNA sequence modeling as an OCR-style visual document understanding problem is a creative conceptual departure from standard 1D token-based LLM architectures, effectively leveraging recent advances in visual document processing.

Comprehensive pretraining task formulation: The paper designs six structured prompt families (T1–T6) spanning fundamental genomic operations (reading, region grounding, ROI transcription, masked span completion, subsequence retrieval, and chromosome classification) with rigorously specified instruction-response protocols and data augmentations (e.g., tail truncation, span sampling).

Strong empirical performance across diverse scales: OpticalDNA demonstrates competitive or superior performance across multiple benchmarks—from eQTL prediction on DNALONGBENCH (outperforming Caduceus and JanusDNA with a fraction of trainable parameters) to cross-subspecies transfer on RiceSubBench and whole-genome phenotype prediction on RiceWGPB against massive foundation models like Evo-2 (7B) and LucaOne (1.8B).

Extensive analysis and reproducibility: The appendix provides extensive details regarding rendering configurations, exact prompt templates, hyperparameter grids, task-specific metrics, ablations against the DeepSeek-OCR baseline, and Grad-CAM interpretability visualizations.
weaknesses: Artificial 2D inductive bias: Rasterizing 1D linear biological polymers into a 2D page introduces artificial 2D vertical adjacencies between nucleotides that are distant along the sequence, while severing linear continuity across line wraps. The paper does not thoroughly explore how downstream performance and representation fidelity vary with arbitrary rendering hyperparameters (e.g., canvas width, line length, typography, or alternative packing strategies like Hilbert/Peano space-filling curves).

Confounding factors in the 1D vs. 2D baseline comparison: In Appendix A (Table S2), lightweight TIMM 2D CNN backbones (MobileNetV3, TinyNet, ResNet-10t) are compared against custom 1D CNNs. It is unclear whether these TIMM backbones were initialized from ImageNet pre-trained weights while the 1D CNNs were trained from scratch; if pre-trained, the observed accuracy and optimization benefits may partially stem from generic pre-trained visual feature priors rather than the 2D layout itself.

Downstream transfer mechanism disconnect: Pretraining primarily optimizes an MoE autoregressive decoder across conversational OCR tasks, yet for downstream tasks, this decoder is discarded entirely. Instead, downstream probing relies exclusively on the visual encoder features (where the primary visual backbone SAM-Conv-CLIP-L was kept frozen during pretraining). An ablation showing representation quality before vs. after pretraining across all tasks would better isolate the impact of the multi-task pretraining objective on the encoder features.

Details on whole-genome processing scale: At ~1,800 nucleotides per page, a ~400M-base genome corresponds to over 200,000 page images. The manuscript reports an inference time of 12.3 minutes for this scale, but lacks sufficient procedural details on how such large document streams are batched, chunked, and mean-pooled across GPUs during feature extraction.

strengths: Highly original and provocative formulation: Recasting biological sequence modeling as visual document understanding and OCR offers an unconventional alternative to standard 1D language modeling paradigms.

Well-structured pretraining framework: The design of six OCR-inspired genomic primitives (T1–T6: transcription, spatial grounding, ROI reading, masked span completion, subsequence retrieval, and chromosome classification) mapped into a unified multimodal conversational format is systematically developed.

Extensive experimental suite: The paper evaluates across diverse biological scales and tasks, spanning tissue eQTL prediction on DNALONGBENCH, phylogeny-aware cross-subspecies transfer on RiceSubBench, and organism-level phenotype modeling on RiceWGPB.

Comprehensive documentation and ablation: The supplementary material provides extensive implementation details, prompt formats, parameter counts, task definitions, and interpretability visualizations using Grad-CAM.
weaknesses: Questionable biological and architectural inductive bias: Rendering 1D symbolic nucleotide sequences ({A, C, G, T}) into 2D raster images introduces hundreds of redundant pixels per base pair and creates artificial 2D spatial adjacencies dictated solely by font size and line wrapping (e.g., characters on adjacent rows are ~60–80 bp apart in sequence space). There is no biological basis for this vertical spatial correlation, and motif structures crossing line wraps are arbitrarily fractured.

Misleading parameter and efficiency framing: The claim that OpticalDNA surpasses baselines with 'up to 985× more activated parameters while tuning only 256k trainable parameters' conflates probe size with model capacity. Inference still requires extracting representations via a 409M-parameter visual backbone; comparing the parameter count of a frozen linear probe (256k) against the full parameter count of baseline models (e.g., 252M) presents an unfair comparison.

Severe underperformance on core pretraining primitives: Several of the proposed OCR primitives perform poorly upon closer inspection. In Table S24, subsequence retrieval (T5) on HG38 achieves a detection accuracy below 5% at IoU ≥ 0.5 and below 0.6% at IoU ≥ 0.99, indicating failure in spatial grounding. Similarly, for masked completion (T4, Table S26), text exact match collapses to <1% for spans ≥ 6 bp, performing near random chance on 4-letter alphabets.

Statistical fragility and evaluation protocol on whole-genome phenotypes: The RiceWGPB benchmark consists of extremely small sample sizes (N = 102 for LRI-15SZ with 21 test samples; N = 130 for TGW with 26 test samples). Predicting complex polygenic traits from whole genomes on ~20 test individuals without reporting confidence intervals, repeated splits, or controls for population stratification leaves the phenotype prediction gains statistically uncertain.

Suboptimal baseline pooling: Baselines such as Evo-2 (7B) and LucaOne (1.8B) are evaluated by naively mean-pooling embeddings across arbitrarily chunked disjoint fragments (70kb and 1.28kb, respectively) over the entire genome, which tends to dilute sequence-level regulatory signals and does not represent a competitive whole-genome aggregation protocol.

strengths: Unorthodox and creative paradigm: Recasting genomic sequence modeling as an OCR-style visual document understanding problem is a novel conceptual angle that departs distinctly from conventional 1D sequence-modeling paradigms.

Comprehensive pretraining task suite: The design of six distinct prompt-conditioned tasks (T1–T6) spanning reading, grounding, ROI transcription, masked completion, and retrieval offers a well-formalized framework for evaluating multimodal document understanding on biological sequences.

Extensive empirical experiments and ablation: The manuscript evaluates the model across multiple benchmarks (DNALONGBENCH eQTL, cross-subspecies splice prediction on RiceSubBench, and whole-genome phenotype prediction), complemented by thorough ablations on OCR fidelity and Grad-CAM interpretability.
weaknesses: Questionable biological inductive bias of 2D text rendering: DNA is a linear sequence whose physical 2D/3D structure arises from biophysical folding (e.g., chromatin loops, secondary structure). Rasterizing DNA as monospace text with arbitrary line wrapping introduces artificial vertical spatial adjacencies (between positions $i$ and $i+W$) that possess no biological relevance, while simultaneously breaking continuous sequence context across line ends.

Information bottleneck for single-nucleotide resolution: Functional genomics and eQTL prediction frequently depend on single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Projecting dense text onto a 640x640 canvas followed by 16x patch downsampling poses a significant risk of aliasing and information loss. This vulnerability is reflected in the pretraining results: masked span recovery drops drastically to <1% exact match for 8-bp spans (Table S26), and subsequence localization Det-Acc@IoU>=0.5 is under 5% on HG38 (Table S24).

Ambiguity in downstream feature pooling for eQTL tasks: The paper states that downstream prediction extracts per-page features, mean-pools across pages, flattens, and applies a linear/MLP probe. For sequences spanning tens to hundreds of pages (e.g., 226 pages in Table 7), mean-pooling across all pages risks washing out localized variant effects that determine eQTL outcomes.

Uncontrolled CNN baseline comparisons (Appendix A): The claim that 2D CNNs inherently outperform 1D CNNs on genomic sequences relies on comparing TIMM 2D architectures (MobileNetV3, TinyNet, ResNet) against basic 1D CNNs lacking dilated convolutions or large receptive fields (standard in modern genomic CNNs like Enformer/BPNet). Furthermore, the paper does not clarify whether the 2D CNNs utilized ImageNet pretraining, which would confound the comparison.

High variance and small sample size on whole-genome phenotype benchmark: The RiceWGPB benchmark operates on extremely small sample sizes (91 training / 26 test samples for TGW; 71 training / 21 test samples for LRI) to predict quantitative traits from whole genomes (~400M bp). Drawing definitive conclusions about whole-genome predictive superiority from such small sample sets is statistically precarious.

strengths: Bold and highly original conceptual formulation: recasting long-range DNA sequence modeling as a visual document understanding / OCR problem provides a fresh perspective that challenges conventional 1D autoregressive and masked language modeling paradigms.

Comprehensive and impressive empirical performance: OpticalDNA outperforms competitive and substantially larger genomic foundation models (including HyenaDNA, Caduceus, Nucleotide Transformer v2, GENERator, Evo-2, and LucaOne) across three distinct benchmarks (DNALONGBENCH eQTL prediction, RiceSubBench cross-subspecies transfer, and RiceWGPB whole-genome phenotype prediction).

High parameter and token efficiency: by leveraging visual compression and multi-page fusion, the model operates on nearly 20x fewer effective tokens and achieves superior downstream accuracy with lightweight linear/MLP probes.

Thorough experimental validation and ablations: the authors provide extensive analyses addressing key questions, including controlled 1D vs. 2D comparisons under matched budgets (Appendix A), rendering format and resolution robustness (Section 4.7 and Appendix N), token bottleneck behavior (Appendix L), and rigorous train-test contamination checks (Appendix I).
weaknesses: Arbitrary spatial inductive bias: 2D rasterization inherently introduces artificial vertical adjacencies between nucleotides on adjacent lines (separated by an arbitrary line-wrap length) that carry no biological meaning. Although Appendix B and N demonstrate empirical robustness across different layouts, the biological justification remains somewhat heuristic and primarily motivated by computational convenience.

Disconnection between generative OCR pretraining and downstream probing: OpticalDNA designs a sophisticated 6-task prompt-guided autoregressive decoding framework during pretraining, but downstream genotype-to-phenotype evaluations bypass the decoder entirely and rely only on mean-pooled visual encoder features. An ablation isolating the individual downstream utility of each of the six pretraining objectives (T1–T6) is missing.

Data pre-processing and rasterization overhead: Converting gigabase-scale genomic sequences into image documents introduces I/O and rendering overheads that are not fully accounted for in the end-to-end computational throughput comparisons.

strengths: Original and creative paradigm shift: The paper introduces OpticalDNA, an intriguing framework that reframes long-range genomic sequence modeling as an OCR-style 2D document understanding problem, offering a fresh conceptual alternative to standard 1D autoregressive and masked language models.

Comprehensive pretraining task design: Formulating genomic operations into six prompt-conditioned multimodal primitives (T1–T6 covering free transcription, spatial grounding, ROI transcription, masked completion, subsequence retrieval, and global classification) provides an elegant conversational interface for genomic reasoning.

Extensive experimental evaluation: OpticalDNA demonstrates competitive downstream performance on long-context benchmarks, including 450 kb eQTL prediction (DNALONGBENCH), phylogeny-aware cross-subspecies transfer (RiceSubBench), and whole-genome phenotype prediction (RiceWGPB).

Thorough ablations and controlled comparisons: The manuscript features extensive supplementary analyses, including controlled comparisons against 1D CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers under matched token budgets (Appendix A), rigorous rendering/layout perturbations (Appendix N), token bottleneck evaluations (Appendix L), and train–test contamination analyses (Appendix I).
weaknesses: Biological artificiality of 2D line-wrapping: Rasterizing a 1D polymer into a 2D canvas introduces arbitrary 2D spatial adjacency across vertical lines that lacks biological grounding. While Appendix B clarifies that the 2D layout serves as an efficient computational interface rather than a biological geometry, 2D convolutions inevitably capture vertical neighborhood features that are purely artifacts of the chosen line width and font size.

Performance bottlenecks on fine-grained grounding (T5) and masked completion (T4): The detailed evaluations in Appendix K show that subsequence localization under strict IoU thresholds remains poor (e.g., Det-Acc@IoU>=0.50 of only 0.046 on HG38 in Table S31) and mask completion exact match drops rapidly as span length increases beyond 1–2 bases (Table S33), highlighting that exact nucleotide recovery and precise visual grounding remain challenging for the visual decoder.

Practical overhead of rendering pipelines: Treating genomic sequences as images introduces significant preprocessing overhead (rasterization, text glyph rendering, and high-dimensional image storage/loading) compared to standard integer token arrays, which can become cumbersome when scaling to whole-genome datasets.

Whole-genome representation aggregation: For whole-genome phenotypes (~400M bases requiring hundreds of thousands of pages), the model relies on per-page feature extraction and simple mean-pooling across pages, which may dilute sparse, highly localized causative variants across the massive genome.

strengths: Highly original conceptual reframing: Reframing 1D genomic sequence modeling as an OCR-style visual document understanding problem provides a novel and thought-provoking departure from the prevailing 1D language model and state-space paradigms.

Effective compression and computational scalability for ultra-long contexts: Leveraging 2D visual layouts and compact vision tokens achieves an effective ~20x compression ratio over base-level sequences, enabling computationally efficient processing of long sequences (450 kb GTEx eQTL) and scaling up to whole-genome inputs (~400 Mb).

Strong empirical performance across multiple genomic benchmarks: OpticalDNA consistently outperforms or matches established genomic foundation models—including models with substantially larger parameter counts (e.g., Evo-2 7B, LucaOne 1.8B, JanusDNA, Caduceus)—on regulatory eQTL prediction, cross-subspecies splice site generalization, and whole-genome phenotype prediction.

Comprehensive validation, ablation studies, and robustness analyses: The submission provides thorough empirical grounding, including controlled 1D vs. 2D comparisons under matched token budgets and backbones (Appendix A.4), detailed rendering robustness checks (varying font, text density, margins, aspect ratio in Appendix N), strict contamination audits (Appendix I), and token bottleneck analyses (Appendix L).

Multi-task genomic OCR primitives and interpretability: Formulating pretraining via six structured OCR tasks (reading, grounding, retrieval, span completion, classification) yields fine-grained localized capabilities, supported by biologically aligned Grad-CAM visual attributions on splice junctions.
weaknesses: Artificial 2D spatial locality: Wrapping 1D genomic sequences into 2D pages introduces artificial spatial adjacencies between vertically adjacent lines (e.g., position i and position i + W) that do not reflect biological reality. Although the authors clarify that the 2D layout serves as a computational interface rather than a biological geometry, the 2D patch-based and convolutional front-end inherently imposes 2D inductive biases; a deeper investigation into whether the model learns to suppress spurious vertical correlations would strengthen the paper.

Roundabout nature of pixel rendering for discrete alphabets: Rasterizing a 4-letter symbolic alphabet into high-resolution RGB image canvases (640x640x3) and decoding glyphs introduces preprocessing and image-rendering overhead compared to native 1D discrete compression schemes (e.g., learned multi-scale tokenizers, byte-level BPE, or 1D strided convolutional front-ends).

Limited sample size on whole-genome phenotype benchmark: While the whole-genome phenotype prediction experiment (RiceWGPB) demonstrates practical scalability to ~400 Mb inputs, the dataset size is quite small (N = 102 and N = 130 accessions in Table S23), which limits the statistical confidence of the regression evaluations.

Disentangling the contribution of the pretrained VLM backbone: OpticalDNA builds directly on DeepSeek-OCR (SAM-Conv-CLIP-L visual front-end and a 3B MoE decoder). Although the ablation against vanilla DeepSeek-OCR in Section 4.3 shows clear gains from genomic pretraining, more discussion on how much general document visual features contribute versus purely genomic features would be valuable.
